The recent work centers on release correctness, package identity, native dependency resolution, and simplifying the CLI. I found the roadmap, but some architecture notes already disagree with the latest PRs; I’ll check those claims against the implementation.

Entire’s session search is unavailable because it isn’t logged in. GitHub PR descriptions are available, so I can still assess the week’s changes, with less visibility into the original conversations.

The release model is a real strength: Callisto records the version decision, orders provider effects, and reruns by observing what already landed. That fits its goals well.

I also found a current operational failure: unit/integration CI is green, but the release workflow fails while updating the release PR because a JSON consumer rejects the new `command` field. I’m tracing that boundary; it matters more to v1 readiness than the test count alone.

This checkout is one PR behind GitHub main: #168 merged during the assessment. It removes the tag configuration required by #167 when packages share a name across ecosystems. I’m including that change in the evaluation.

I’m also using the audit skill for a focused check of the JSON failure, so the readiness concern rests on a reachable code path.

content.text:
The JSON failure reproduces locally: `release-pr decide` emits `command` and `dryRun`, then `release-pr verify` rejects them. The existing contract tests check extracted fields but never pass the real output into the real consumer.

The competitor comparison also sharpens Callisto’s position. File-based versioning and Rust support already exist elsewhere. Its strongest distinction is coordinating Cargo, npm, Python, and binary artifacts under an explicit release and recovery model.

There’s a second recovery gap in the local route. After a tag is created, a failed push or GitHub release can leave unfinished work, but the next bare `callisto release` excludes the tagged package and reports nothing left to release. CI retains the committed package roster and can recover through the executor.

The architecture is coherent overall. The remaining risk is concentrated where contracts meet: command output and input, release selection and completion, and the documented guarantees and their actual support boundaries.

Callisto has made substantial progress toward v1. The architecture is coherent, the release model has a clear purpose, and the past week’s work mostly strengthens the right guarantees. I would hold v1 today because two release paths still violate the intended behavior: the managed release PR workflow currently fails, and a bare local retry can omit unfinished work.

The strongest competitive position is **dependency-aware releases across Cargo, npm, Python, and binary artifacts, with explicit source identity and recovery semantics**. Changesets-style input alone is already available elsewhere.

I reviewed the [roadmap](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/docs/projects/ROAD-TO-V1.md), [v1 requirement](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/docs/specs/REQ-DX-V1.md), architecture, implementation, and roughly 60 merged PRs from September 19–26 Pacific. The checkout is at #167; I also inspected #168’s changes on GitHub.

The week’s work follows a coherent direction:

- **Release correctness:** immutable intent, provider observation, recovery without persisted execution state, consistent tag identity, and assets gating product publication. [#101](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/101), [#124](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/124), [#154](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/154).
- **A simpler product:** eight visible commands, one release verb, status showing actual planned bumps, and setup that detects facts and asks intent. Removing credential preflight, shipped features, and the WASM integration also reduced maintenance burden. [#134](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/134), [#136](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/136), [#143](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/143).
- **Native ecosystem correctness:** fixed groups and prereleases, dependency floors, lockfile refreshes, PEP 440 snapshots, and Changesets input compatibility. These address whether the resulting repository actually works with its native tools. [#156](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/156), [#158](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/158), [#161](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/161), [#166](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/166).
- **Identity and maintainability:** one selector resolver, directory identity, historical ownership checks, four published crates, and typed diagnostics. [#160](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/160), [#157](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/157), [#168](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/168).

My assessment is that this was valuable consolidation and correction. The recurring weakness is that individually sound changes can still break their composition.

The four-crate structure is reasonable. Manifest editing, graph policy, and CLI presentation remain separated; dependencies point downward. Consolidation reduces packaging overhead without requiring another decomposition before v1. One naming qualification matters: `callisto-model` now contains Git and file I/O as well as domain types, so it is a foundational crate rather than a purely inert model. That is manageable when documented clearly. [Architecture](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/ARCHITECTURE.md:25).

The semantic model’s best feature is its separation of responsibilities. A package owns a version and changelog; native release identities identify its registry publications; an artifact represents produced bytes; the product determines their GitHub Release destination. The decision records what will release, while intent records how those effects depend on each other. This handles a Cargo/npm package or an asset built by one package and distributed through another without inventing independent versions for every output. [Package model](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/package.rs:14), [release derivation](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/derive.rs:485).

Identity is also improving, but the wording currently overstates the implementation. `PackageKey` represents directory identity; most in-run maps still use `PackageId`, deliberately. #168 preserves earlier release history through ownership checks, while new default tags use the qualified display ID after promotion. “Promotion is display-only” therefore needs qualification: ownership remains stable, but newly generated tag names can change. [Accepted ADR](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/8ef9aa5a4fc01242221fa59dd4cbcb4893794778/docs/adr/0011-directory-keyed-package-identity.md).

The release executor is particularly strong. It distinguishes absence, matching effects, conflicts, and uncertainty; success requires observed evidence; prerequisites control ordering; receipts come from recorded execution evidence. The simulator tests recovery across faults. Those are substantive engineering advantages. The assurance still depends on what each provider proves: registry adoption currently establishes that a version exists, with no package checksum, while binary assets have stronger byte identity checks. [Observations](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/release_observation.rs:23), [executor](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs:26).

Two issues deserve immediate attention:

1. **The release PR workflow is broken on latest main.** `release-pr decide` emits `command` and `dryRun`; the action passes that output unchanged to `release-pr verify`, whose strict input type rejects those fields with E281. I reproduced this using the compiled CLI. Latest main has green CI but a [failed Release run](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/36281315129). The contract tests check jq extraction without exercising this real producer-to-consumer handoff. [Producer](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release_pr.rs:79), [consumer](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release_pr.rs:47).

2. **Bare local release recovery loses unfinished packages after tag creation.** The local route selects packages by tag absence. If tag creation succeeds and its push—or a subsequent forge operation—fails, the next bare release excludes that package. It can report “Nothing to release” despite unfinished effects. CI retains its committed roster and can recover through the executor. This is a reachable code-path finding; I verified the tag-based exclusion with the existing test, but did not dynamically inject the complete failure sequence. [Selection](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:195), [tag effect](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/tag.rs:72).

Against the competitors, the comparison is:

| Tool | Existing strength | Callisto’s opportunity and limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Changesets** | Explicit change files, dependency-aware versioning, fixed/linked groups, prereleases. Its documented non-npm approach still requires `package.json`. [Docs](https://changesets.dev/guide/beyond-npm). | Native Cargo/Python manifests and coordinated publication are meaningful advantages. Accepting change files does not establish configuration or behavioral equivalence; Callisto currently warns about discarded configuration keys. |
| **Knope** | Changesets and commit inference, multiple versioned files, automatic workspace detection, configurable workflows, and draft–upload–publish release assets. [Defaults](https://knope.tech/reference/default-config/), [releases](https://knope.tech/reference/config-file/steps/release/). | The closest conceptual competitor. Callisto offers more prescribed graph and recovery semantics; Knope offers broader workflow flexibility. Draft asset ordering is shared functionality. |
| **Nx Release** | Project graph integration, release groups, commit inference, first-class version-plan files, and a programmatic API. Rust publishing is documented through a plugin. [Version plans](https://nx.dev/docs/guides/nx-release/file-based-versioning-version-plans), [Rust](https://nx.dev/docs/kb/publish-rust-crates). | Callisto can appeal to repositories that want release management without adopting Nx’s workspace tooling. File-based versioning and graph awareness are already competitive requirements. |
| **Release Please** | Maintained release PRs, many language strategies, and Cargo workspace support. It explicitly leaves registry publication to other tooling. [README](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please). | Callisto’s coordinated publication and recovery cover work users otherwise assemble themselves. Release PR automation alone is shared functionality. |

That comparison supports Callisto’s design direction; it does not establish superior real-world reliability.

The remaining evidence is uneven. Native-resolution checks and real local registries are significant improvements, but Cargo/PyPI publication tests exercise less of the complete executor than npm’s test, and several checks skip when prerequisite tools are absent. Generated maturin workflows remain unsupported. The “first published release in under ten minutes” goal has no measured onboarding evidence, and the README’s quick start omits required `--versioning`, commit steps, and credential preparation. [Registry tests](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/tests/release_real_registry_e2e_tests.rs), [workflow support](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/init.rs:624).

Documentation also needs another reconciliation. The architecture diagram still says the decision is written before apply; identity documentation describes superseded tag behavior; the requirement still lists Cargo registry testing as missing. These inaccuracies affect the guarantees maintainers and users think they have.

My recommended order is:

1. Fix the two release failures and test the complete command handoffs, including local failure after tag creation.
2. Complete a real self-release and exercise first-release setup in representative fresh repositories.
3. Reconcile documentation and state the v1 support boundaries precisely, especially Python bindings, generated workflows, migration, formatting, and recovery.
4. Finish the remaining declared guarantees and owner decisions before expanding platform scope. Separate reachable correctness problems from hardening items such as the currently test-only group constructor.

I would preserve the current architecture and focus the next work on those boundaries. Callisto already has a credible design; v1 needs convincing evidence that users can complete the promised lifecycle.

No repository files changed. Local verification included a build, ten release-command tests, the tag-selection test, and the reproduced E281 failure. Entire transcript history was unavailable because authentication was missing, so historical intent came from PR descriptions and repository documents.

Claude found this that you seem to have missed:

No, don't merge #113. It won't release anything, because the Release workflow on main is broken and #113 is stale.

- The failure: the Release workflow has failed on every merge since #166 (the runs for #166, #167 and #168). It dies in the "Create or update the Callisto release PR" step with E281 --decision is not valid JSON: unknown field command.
- The cause: #166 put release-pr decide --format json output inside the shared JSON wrapper, which adds command and dryRun fields. create-or-update-release-pr.sh passes that output straight to release-pr verify --decision, which rejects fields it doesn't know. No test runs that pair: the binary contract test calls decide but never passes the result to verify.
- #113 is out of date: it was generated from #163, so it lacks #166, #167 and #168 and its release-decision.json is from before them. The bot can't refresh it until the workflow is fixed. Merging it now would publish 0.9.0 without the identity and v1 fixes.
- The publish path looks safe from the same bug: release plan, artifact-manifest and release write their intent, manifest and receipt files without the wrapper, so it shouldn't recur there. I've only read the code, though; the publish jobs haven't run since #166.

Proposed fix, as one small PR done directly:
1. Make release-pr verify --decision accept decide's output as-is, ignoring the wrapper fields. That's more robust than having the script strip them.
2. Extend test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh so it pipes decide into verify.
3. Add a patch changeset.

Once that merges, the bot regenerates #113 from current main. You approve its CI and merge, and 0.9.0 goes out. Go?

On the Codex text you pasted: it's about the plugins repo (voice.md, dist/codex, versions for ranger, scribe and muse), not Callisto. I haven't acted on it. If it was meant for this session, say what you want; otherwise it probably belongs in the session working on the plugins repo.

And it also said of your input:

For v0.9, Codex's review changes nothing: E281 is the only blocker. It found the same bug independently. Its second finding is real, but it's a v1 item, not a v0.9 one.

1. Release PR workflow broken (E281): this blocks v0.9. The fix is what I proposed: verify accepts decide's output as-is, plus a test that pipes decide into verify.

2. A retried local release can skip unfinished work: real (I checked the code), but it doesn't affect v0.9.
- derive_unreleased_decision (release_decision.rs:195) skips every package whose current version already has a tag, and it counts local tags.
- If a local callisto release creates the tag and then the push or the GitHub Release fails, a retry skips that package and reports nothing left to release.
- v0.9 goes through CI, which releases exactly the packages in the committed release-decision.json, so this path isn't used.
- It is a real v1 gap. One fix: when a package's tag exists, still check its remaining steps (push, GitHub Release, assets) instead of skipping it. I haven't designed this in detail yet.

3. Its other points are v1 work, not v0.9 blockers. I haven't verified each one yet:

content.text:
Yes—that failure stopped the bot from refreshing #113. The [linked run](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/actions/runs/36281315129) confirms the exact sequence:

1. `release-pr decide --format json` produces a decision.
2. Versioning successfully computes 0.9.0 and updates files **inside the runner**.
3. Before updating the remote release branch, the script passes that decision to `release-pr verify`.
4. Verification fails with E281: `unknown field command`. The runner exits, so its regenerated files never reach #113.

The regression came from #166: `decide` now emits the shared JSON envelope, including `command` and `dryRun`, but `verify` still expects the bare decision schema. This is a producer/consumer contract mismatch—not malformed JSON, credentials, or publishing trouble.

What we need to fix:

- Make `verify --decision` accept `decide`’s output unchanged. Accept the known envelope fields at the CLI boundary while preserving strict decision and snapshot validation; don’t broadly disable unknown-field checks.
- Extend [the binary contract test](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/callisto-action/tests/test_release_pr_decide_binary_contract.sh) to pass real `decide` output into real `verify`. Cover create/update and ensure a changed snapshot still fails.
- Add a patch changeset, merge the fix, and let a **new main workflow run** regenerate #113. Rerunning the old failed run would still use the broken revision.

One correction to the earlier assessment: **#113’s source code is now current.** Its latest commit merges main at `8ef9aa5`, including #166–#168. But merging main into the branch does not regenerate its release decision, consume newer changesets, or refresh its changelogs. Source freshness and release-metadata freshness are different.

Also, E281 breaks the **release-PR refresh path**, not necessarily publication after merging a recognized release PR—the publish jobs take a different workflow branch. Nevertheless, I recommend fixing this and regenerating #113 before merging it, so 0.9 ships a working release workflow and complete release metadata.

Anything else that changes in the last week's worth of PRs that we forgot to adjust in the rest of the system? I feel like Claude lost the plot a bit there and started focusing on micro fixes vs the system as a whole. Check for me, very thoroughly

I’ll trace the last week’s changes across the whole release lifecycle: identity, versioning, release decisions, execution, workflows, and documentation. I’ll look for places where one layer changed but its consumers or guarantees didn’t, and separate confirmed defects from design gaps.

content.text:
The strongest pattern is now clear: several paths still assume “one package = one ecosystem,” while the new model allows multiple manifests and names per directory. That affects dependency rewrites, lockfiles, release ordering, and retry recovery—not just documentation.

I’m also checking the generated customer workflows separately. Callisto’s own durable release workflow does not exercise every path that `init` gives users.

I’ve reproduced failures across versioning, committed release verification, Python prereleases, and historical tag lookup. The relevant existing suites still pass: 35 tests covering release execution, durable releases, schemas, and identity promotion.

That points to a coverage gap at the joins. The tests mostly verify each stage separately, not whether one stage’s real output remains valid input to the next.

One more recovery failure turned out to be real. With a changeset freshly created by `callisto add`, a failed lockfile refresh occurs after the version and changelog are written and the changeset is deleted. The error says to rerun `version`, but that rerun reports no pending changesets; with `--emit-decision`, it instead fails because the release roster is empty.

This needs explicit partial-run handling. It does not require abandoning the agreed no-journal policy.

Yes. There are several missed system-level adjustments—not just documentation cleanup.

**E281 explains the broken release-PR refresh. Fixing it does not establish product-wide v0.9 readiness.** The broader pattern is that Callisto’s core model has advanced, but some consumers still encode older assumptions: one package has one ecosystem, a tag means release completion, and a version string carries enough semantic information.

I reviewed the week’s merged PRs and affected callers, workflows, schemas, tests, specs, and ADRs. I also built current main through #168 in an isolated snapshot and reproduced failures in temporary Git repositories. No tracked repository files changed.

## 1. The multi-manifest model is not consistently respected

This is the most important architectural finding.

Callisto correctly models one directory as one package, with several canonical manifests and native release identities. However, two execution paths still reduce that package to a single ecosystem.

**Dependency rewrites can change behavior after display-ID promotion.**

I reproduced this arrangement:

- One directory contains Cargo `app` and npm `@scope/app`.
- It depends on another dual-manifest directory containing Cargo `core` and npm `@scope/core`.
- Adding a separate npm `app` promotes the original display ID to `cargo/app`.
- Versioning then tries to rewrite the npm dependency using `core`, not `@scope/core`, and fails with E017.

The shared helper prefers the display ID’s ecosystem over the dependency edge’s actual manifest. It also serves dependency-floor and snapshot rewrites, so those siblings need the same correction. The failed version run had already written some Cargo changes; retry then encountered the partial-run guard. [Source](crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs) is [cascade.rs:160](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs:160).

**Lockfile refresh misses secondary ecosystems.**

In another dual Cargo/npm fixture, `version` successfully changed both manifests from `1.0.0` to `1.0.1`, but refreshed only Cargo’s lockfile. The npm lockfile remained at `1.0.0`.

The implementation selects one ecosystem per bump—even when that bump has several manifest writes. That undermines #158’s native-resolution guarantee. [apply.rs:368](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:368)

The structural correction is straightforward: derive ecosystem context from each actual manifest or write target. A display/selector prefix must not choose execution semantics. This does **not** require re-keying every in-memory map by `PackageKey`.

## 2. Release completion is still confused with intermediate progress

The previously identified retry bug is broader than “local releases.”

After tag creation succeeds but push or GitHub Release creation fails, bare `release` derives a new roster, sees the tag, and excludes the entire package. I reproduced:

1. First release fails during push.
2. The local annotated tag remains.
3. The identical retry exits successfully with “Nothing to release.”
4. No successful receipt exists.

The generated **simple customer workflow** uses this same bare-release path. Callisto’s own durable workflow retains the committed roster, so its selection path avoids this particular problem. [release_decision.rs:195](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:195), [init.rs:785](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/init.rs:785)

There is a related multi-manifest ordering problem.

For a package publishing to Cargo, npm, and GitHub, the actual generated operation order allowed:

`Cargo publish → shared tag → GitHub release → npm publish`

The tag prerequisites include only that registry identity’s publishes, although both identities use the same physical tag and GitHub release. An npm failure can therefore leave a publicly visible release marker for an incompletely published package. The tag-based selector then compounds the problem on retry. This was confirmed from the generated DAG and executor ordering; I did not publish to live registries. [derive.rs:380](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/derive.rs:380)

The missing distinction is between:

- The directory-level package.
- Each native registry identity.
- Shared physical tag/forge effects.
- Completion of the whole required release.

Those should be reconciled as one repair, not separate conditional patches.

## 3. Failed versioning can lose its recoverable input

This is an additional recovery defect, beyond release retries.

I ran `callisto add`, leaving its newly created changeset untracked, then injected a lockfile-refresh failure during `version --emit-decision`.

The result was:

- Manifest and changelog written.
- Changeset deleted.
- Lock refresh failed with E208.
- No release decision written.
- Changes remained unstaged.

The diagnostic recommends rerunning `version`. But:

- Bare retry exits successfully with no pending changesets.
- Retry with `--emit-decision` fails with E160 because the roster is empty.

Changeset deletion precedes the fallible refresh/staging steps. Meanwhile, partial-run detection checks changesets at HEAD or staged manifests, missing this interrupted state. [apply.rs:328](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:328), [version.rs:313](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/version.rs:313)

The agreed no-journal policy can remain. But inputs must remain recoverable, interrupted states must be detected consistently, and recovery instructions must describe an operation the CLI can actually perform.

## 4. Python version semantics do not survive storage

Two independently reproduced failures share one cause: stable strings such as `1.0.1` are valid under both SemVer and PEP 440.

**Committed release decisions fail verification.**

Python versioning successfully emitted and committed a decision for `1.0.1`. `release plan` then rejected it with E165: manifest version does not match the claimed version—even though both strings were `1.0.1`.

The decision decoder reconstructed SemVer; the historical Python manifest reader reconstructed PEP 440. Their typed versions were unequal.

**Stable Python prerelease baselines fail the next bump.**

`pre enter beta` succeeded from a stable Python version. After adding a patch changeset, `version` failed with E037 because the stored baseline had reloaded as SemVer while the bump operation required PEP 440.

[Version decoding](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/version.rs:163), [prerelease decoding](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/format/pre.rs:84)

The model already carries grammar, and release identities already carry ecosystem. The gap is context-aware decoding. Fix the decision and prerelease consumers together, then audit the other persisted version-bearing contracts. Globally changing the parser’s preference—or comparing only rendered strings—would conceal the semantic problem.

## 5. Versioning supports outputs that release verification rejects

Two further end-to-end mismatches:

**Inherited Cargo versions.** `version` correctly updated `[workspace.package].version`, emitted the member’s decision, and updated its changelog. After committing, `release plan` failed with E164 because the member manifest had no literal version.

The historical reader explicitly refuses inheritance. There is also a second obstacle: verification requires the member manifest itself in the diff, although the legitimate version edit belongs to the workspace root. Fixing just the reader would be incomplete. [release_decision.rs:580](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:580)

**Root packages.** For ordinary single-package repositories, the default changelog path is `./CHANGELOG.md`, while Git reports `CHANGELOG.md`. A valid version commit consequently fails E165 because the verifier says the changelog was untouched. I reproduced this with Cargo and Python root packages. [release_decision.rs:440](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:440)

These need shared historical **effective-version/source-path resolution** and canonical workspace-relative paths. That preserves committed-decision authority without re-running bump policy.

## 6. #168 fixes ordinary promotion, but not historical identity transitions

The new promotion tests pass. Three other transitions do not:

| Transition | Reproduced result |
| --- | --- |
| An existing npm sibling is renamed from `bar` to `foo` | Cargo `foo` loses its earlier bare release tag |
| A new Cargo manifest is added to an existing npm directory, followed by a same-named sibling | The original directory loses its earlier tag |
| A promoted package releases as `cargo/foo@1.1.0`, then its sibling is removed | Lookup falls back to the older `foo@1.0.0` |

Historical ownership currently checks whether the **first current canonical manifest’s path** existed at the old revision. It does not establish what name that manifest declared historically, and it overlooks other canonical manifests.

Demotion also stops searching the qualified namespace. That can give inference an obsolete release baseline.

[Historical ownership on current main](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/8ef9aa5a4fc01242221fa59dd4cbcb4893794778/crates/callisto-graph/src/lib.rs#L217), [tag lookup](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/blob/8ef9aa5a4fc01242221fa59dd4cbcb4893794778/crates/callisto-graph/src/tags.rs#L156)

Directory identity is a sound foundation. Historical ownership still needs historical declarations, the full manifest roster, and continuity across both promotion and demotion.

## 7. JSON contracts and generated workflows have incomplete follow-through

**E281 is one producer–consumer contract failure.** The report wrapper changed, but the action still feeds that report directly into a strict durable-document decoder.

**Published schemas also disagree with actual wire output.** Generated schemas describe `PackageId` and `Version` as objects, while real status output serializes them as strings. Receipt identities have the same representation mismatch. The schema tests check selected structure, not whether complete real outputs satisfy their schemas. [schema.rs:13](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/schema.rs:13)

Generated customer workflows have additional gaps. These are source-traced; I did not execute complete hosted workflows:

- **Napi builds are workspace-wide, not release-intent-scoped.** Cargo artifact rows are selected from intent slots, but napi rows and placement visit every addon. An unrelated addon can block a Cargo-only release. [init.rs:853](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/init.rs:853)
- **Authentication wiring retained ineffective token names.** Templates export `PYPI_TOKEN`, rather than Twine’s native credentials, and export `NPM_TOKEN` without configuring npm authentication. Existing manual auth configuration can make this work; secrets alone do not. Callisto’s publishing guide correctly documents the missing setup. [Generated environment](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/init.rs:1078), [Twine documentation](https://twine.readthedocs.io/en/stable/), [npm documentation](https://docs.npmjs.com/using-private-packages-in-a-ci-cd-workflow/)
- **Init accepts product artifacts the generated matrix cannot build.** I reproduced init accepting an npm executable and creating artifact slots, while `matrix` returned no corresponding entries. Workflow generation accepts that shape, but its slot join only finds Cargo build entries. [Support check](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/init.rs:624), [matrix filter](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/matrix.rs:62)

Two smaller source-confirmed onboarding issues also deserve follow-up: Cargo binary detection misses `src/bin`-only executables, and the installer chooses a local build whenever the root manifest merely contains `callisto-cli`, bypassing the requested pinned version. [Binary inventory](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-manifests/src/cargo.rs:229), [installer heuristic](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.github/actions/setup-callisto/scripts/install-callisto.sh:143)

## Documentation drift is operational, not cosmetic

Several documents now prescribe the wrong behavior:

- The architecture diagram and ADR 2 still say the decision is written before apply.
- Versioning architecture says a crashed run can be rerun, while the CLI deliberately refuses some partial runs.
- Identity documentation says default tags use native names; #168 uses display IDs.
- ADR 11’s “display-only” wording needs qualification because promotion changes new default tag names.
- The matrix spec explicitly forbids the `command` field that the unified JSON wrapper adds.
- README’s quick start omits required versioning selection and the commit step before release.

These contradictions make future fixes more likely to preserve the wrong assumption.

One unresolved **policy choice**, not an automatic bug fix: inference-only packages can have a pending inferred bump, while release-PR automation returns “no pending changesets,” and committed verification requires a consumed changeset. The release spec explicitly requires that changeset. Decide whether inference augments changesets or supports fully changeset-free automation before changing authorization rules.

## What I would tackle

I would organize this into coherent repair batches:

1. **Wire contracts:** E281, real producer-to-consumer round trips, context-aware Python decoding, and schemas validated against actual output.
2. **Manifest context:** dependency rewrites, snapshot/floor siblings, and refresh/staging for every touched ecosystem.
3. **Completion and recovery:** shared publish barriers, unfinished release selection, and recoverable partial version runs.
4. **Historical verification:** inherited Cargo versions, canonical paths, and promotion/demotion ownership.
5. **Generated workflow conformance:** intent-scoped builds, native auth setup, truthful supported shapes, and documentation reconciliation.

For v0.9, I would prioritize the reproducible public-command correctness failures above documentation-only polish. E281 remains the immediate unblocker for Callisto’s own release, but I disagree with categorizing all the others as safely deferrable v1 work: several already break supported everyday flows.

The architecture does not need wholesale replacement. Its crate boundaries, committed authority, sealed intents, and observation-based executor are good foundations. **The missing work is enforcing those semantics consistently across boundaries.**

All **35 targeted existing tests passed** on current main. That is why the next testing investment should be complete public lifecycles—`add → version → commit → plan → execute → late failure → retry`—across root packages, inherited versions, Python prereleases, dual manifests, and identity transitions. A successful self-release proves one important configuration; it does not prove the whole product.

I did not run full `just ci`, live publishing, or complete generated GitHub workflows.

Should we just use canonical IDs vs allowing the flex ones then? This avoids future confusion when adding new ones and it simplifies the mental model for our users. It doesn't sound as simple to start but the magic might be more confusing (and it complicates our code).

Should NPM publish happent before tag and GH release? Should we consider it as a graph as we add more languages and the possibility of cross dependencies? Could a NPM package depend on a RS crate and a PyPi package? Or in the future a Go package or Nuget package? Is it possible for a Nuget package to depend on rust, go, or python? or vice-versa?

I’ll separate package identity from release ordering, then check what cross-language dependencies actually mean in the package managers. That should clarify where canonical IDs simplify things and where Callisto needs a richer graph.

I’m using the research skill because this is a design choice, not just a bug fix. I’ll distinguish native package-manager dependencies from build, binding, and runtime relationships; they need different release rules.

Two distinctions matter here. Canonical ecosystem/name IDs would remove name promotion, but one source project can still produce several packages. And publication order cannot be universally “registries, then tags”: Go commonly publishes module versions through Git tags. The graph needs to distinguish publication prerequisites from shared release-completion markers.

content.text:
**Yes—I would remove automatic bare/qualified ID promotion. And yes, release ordering should come from a graph—but a graph with explicit kinds of relationships, not one generic “depends on” edge.**

The distinction that matters most is: **a source project, a published package, and a release are not necessarily the same thing.**

## Canonical IDs: simpler, with one important separation

I would use qualified IDs consistently:

```text
cargo/core
npm/@acme/core
pypi/acme-core
nuget/Acme.Core
```

They should not change spelling because another package was added. New configuration, generated changesets, and machine-readable output should use these exact identities.

But one directory can produce several of those packages. Its internal identity should remain separate:

| Concept | Identity |
| --- | --- |
| Source project | Workspace directory, such as `crates/core` |
| Published distribution | `cargo/core`, `npm/@acme/core`, etc. |
| Publication | Distribution + registry destination + version |
| Shared release | Explicit owner/group of the distributions and artifacts being announced |

This makes the user-facing rule straightforward: **names are always qualified; outputs that belong together are explicitly associated.**

It also prevents the bug we found: even if a project is addressed through `cargo/app`, a dependency in its `package.json` is still an npm dependency. Qualification alone does not fix that—execution must use the actual manifest context.

Callisto already has an exact `ReleasePackageId`; I would extend that discipline rather than keep flexible matching throughout the system. [Current exact identity type](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs:45)

Because Changesets compatibility is a goal, I would retain **legacy import handling**, not wildcard identities in the core. Resolve old bare references once at the boundary, reject ambiguity, and emit canonical references thereafter. Existing tags and prerelease records need an explicit migration; removing promotion does not erase their history.

## Should npm publish before the tag and GitHub release?

**For an ordinary Callisto release, yes: all required package publications should succeed and be confirmed before its shared tag and public GitHub announcement.**

For a release with Cargo, npm, and Python outputs:

```text
Verified builds
    ├── crates.io publication ──┐
    ├── npm publication ────────┤
    └── PyPI publication ───────┘
                  │
         All required publications confirmed
                  │
             Shared release tag
                  │
        GitHub draft / asset uploads
                  │
          Publish GitHub release
                  │
             Success receipt
```

Independent publications can run concurrently; real prerequisites determine ordering. This barrier belongs to **that release unit**, not necessarily the entire workspace.

Two qualifications:

- Publishing across registries is not atomic. If Cargo succeeds and npm fails, Cargo remains published. Retry must observe and finish the incomplete work—not discard the roster because a tag exists.
- **Not every tag is a completion marker.** Go commonly publishes module versions through Git tags. A Go version tag is itself a publication operation, potentially required before a downstream operation. A universal “every registry before every tag” rule would therefore be wrong. [Go publication documentation](https://go.dev/doc/modules/publishing)

## Can packages depend across languages?

**Yes at the software level. Not usually as ordinary cross-registry dependency entries.**

Package managers resolve their own package formats: npm does not automatically install a PyPI dependency, and NuGet does not automatically resolve a Cargo crate. A bridge must define how the foreign component is built, packaged, installed, or accessed. [npm dependencies](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-json/), [Python dependency specification](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-specifiers/), [NuGet dependencies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/reference/nuspec)

Common arrangements include:

| Relationship | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| npm uses Rust | Build a native Node addon, then distribute it through npm. [napi-rs](https://napi.rs/docs/introduction/getting-started) |
| Python uses Rust | Build a Python extension and package it in a wheel. [Maturin](https://www.maturin.rs/tutorial) |
| NuGet uses Rust or Go | Package a compatible native library and call its exported interface from .NET. NuGet supports native assets; Go can produce C-compatible shared libraries. [NuGet native assets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/create-packages/native-files-in-net-packages), [Go build modes](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Build_modes) |
| .NET uses Python | Embed a Python runtime and import modules, or invoke a separate Python process. Runtime and Python dependency provisioning remain necessary. [Python.NET](https://pythonnet.github.io/pythonnet/dotnet.html) |
| Python uses .NET | Load a .NET runtime through Python.NET. [Documentation](https://pythonnet.github.io/pythonnet/python.html) |
| Rust/Go use .NET | Expose a suitable native interface, host the runtime, or communicate through a process/service boundary. Native AOT can expose .NET libraries to non-.NET callers. [Microsoft documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/libraries) |

So an npm package can use **both Rust and Python**: for example, a Rust addon plus a Python worker. But npm installation does not automatically establish the Python environment. That needs an explicit distribution/runtime strategy.

Likewise, a NuGet package can contain or call Rust, Go, or Python components. The relationship is possible; the packaging, ABI, platform, and runtime requirements are what make it workable.

**Language and distribution ecosystem are different axes.** Rust code can be distributed through npm, PyPI, or NuGet without consumers ever installing its Cargo package.

## What graph should Callisto model?

Callisto already has a release-operation graph with prerequisites. The missing work is accurately deriving it from richer relationships. [Operation model](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs:1244)

I would distinguish these relationships:

| Relationship | What it implies |
| --- | --- |
| Native package dependency | Native version-range handling; publication ordering when the consumer requires a newly published dependency |
| Embedded/build input | Rebuild the consumer; upstream registry publication may be unnecessary |
| External runtime/service dependency | Compatibility requirements; not automatically release ordering |
| Version coupling | Explicit shared-version or bump-propagation policy |
| Shared release ownership | A completion barrier across required outputs and assets |

The crucial example:

**An npm addon built from a local Rust crate needs that crate’s source/build output. It does not necessarily need the crate published to crates.io first.**

Conversely, a Cargo package whose published manifest requires a new crates.io version does need that version available before publication.

Treating both as the same edge creates unnecessary publications, over-ordering, and potentially artificial cycles. Runtime dependency graphs can also contain cycles; the executable operation graph must remain schedulable or report a concrete unsupported cycle.

Version impact needs its own policy too. A breaking Rust change does not automatically mean an npm wrapper needs a major release—the wrapper might absorb the change without altering its public API.

## My recommendation for Callisto

I would adopt three principles:

1. **Canonical identities everywhere; compatibility aliases only at input boundaries.**
2. **Explicit source-to-distribution ownership and typed dependency relationships.**
3. **An operation DAG that follows actual prerequisites, with shared release completion and retry independent of tag existence.**

For v1, implement those principles for Cargo, npm, and Python first. Keep builds delegated to their tools, and add cross-project relationships only where there is a concrete supported use case. Go and NuGet should later supply their native identity, version, publication, and dependency semantics—not inherit Rust-shaped assumptions.

That is a simplification of the mental model without pretending all ecosystems behave identically. It removes the surprising magic while preserving Callisto’s strongest differentiator: coordinating releases across different kinds of packages.

This sounds good. We can scope the work to what is most relevant right now for rust, npm/pnpm, python/pypi but make sure our architecture and model can support the complications when we add go and C#/NuGet/.NET

I’ll turn that direction into a scoped requirement: Rust, npm/pnpm, and Python/PyPI now, with model boundaries that don’t assume future Go or .NET releases behave the same way. I’ll check the existing roadmap and requirements first so we don’t create a competing plan.
I’m using the requirement-capture skill to keep the scope explicit. Go and .NET should shape the contracts now, but they won’t become required implementations or release gates for this work.

Agreed. **Implement the current ecosystems; make future differences representable without implementing them yet.** I’d fold this into the existing `REQ-DX-V1`, not create a separate ecosystem-expansion project.

Proposed scope draft:

```json
{
  "id": "REQ-DX-V1",
  "statement": "Make Rust/Cargo, npm/pnpm, and Python/PyPI releases predictable, with contracts that can accommodate Go and .NET/NuGet.",
  "stakeholder": "Maintainers of single-ecosystem and polyglot repositories",
  "why": "Identity ambiguity and conflated dependency relationships make workspace growth and release recovery surprising.",
  "done_when": [
    "New references use canonical qualified IDs, with an explicit migration for existing references.",
    "Source projects, distributions, publication destinations, and shared release ownership remain distinct.",
    "Current workflows preserve native version semantics and refresh every affected ecosystem's lockfiles.",
    "Committed decisions remain valid through planning and execution.",
    "Release ordering follows actual prerequisites; retries complete unfinished work.",
    "Generated workflows operate only on selected release outputs.",
    "Model examples represent Go tag-based publication and NuGet native assets without imposing current ecosystem assumptions."
  ],
  "out_of_scope": [
    "Production Go or .NET/NuGet adapters",
    "A universal build system or cross-language package manager",
    "Automatic discovery of arbitrary cross-language dependencies"
  ]
}
```

The architectural guardrails are:

- An embedded Rust build input is not automatically a crates.io publication prerequisite.
- Version coupling is explicit; a dependency change does not automatically dictate a consumer’s bump.
- Versions retain their native grammar.
- Tags can serve different purposes; tag existence never universally means completion.
- Shared provider effects have one owner, even when several distributions participate.

I’d start with the identity/ownership ADR and dependency-to-operation contracts, then repair the current adapters and verify complete lifecycles. Go and .NET remain **design examples**, not shipped support or additional release gates.

This is a draft scope only; I haven’t changed the repository.

Does this account for all the variations you thought through? Any research and checking you need to do? Look for prior art, check what our polyglot comptetition does? Understand the corner cases and differences between the systems? We don't want to over-engineer though.

I’ll check the proposed scope against prior art and ecosystem edge cases, including Knope and Nx’s polyglot support. I’ll separate what Callisto needs now from future complications that only need room in the model.

I’m using the research skill to check the design against official docs and implementations. One point I want to test carefully is version ownership: a Rust project that produces npm packages or Python wheels may have one release version, several native encodings, and multiple artifacts. We shouldn’t expose all of that as extra user configuration unless it’s necessary.

Not completely. The direction holds, but the research exposed gaps we should account for before implementation. **Canonical IDs simplify identity; they do not, by themselves, solve version ownership, dependency meaning, or release completion.**

I checked official documentation and relevant competitor implementations, then tested two fresh Cargo/Python layouts against the main #168 binary. No repository files were changed.

## What the competition teaches us

| Tool | Relevant approach | Lesson for Callisto |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Changesets | npm-focused package graph, with pnpm support. Its publisher processes dependency-ordered batches and subsequently tags successful publications, including successes from a partially failed run. | Borrow native dependency handling and partial-success recovery—not a polyglot abstraction it doesn’t provide. [Implementation](https://github.com/changesets/changesets/blob/main/packages/cli/src/commands/publish/index.ts) |
| Knope | One release package can own several versioned files, including Cargo and Python manifests. However, its documented Python support does not include dependency updates. | A simple user-facing release unit can contain several distributions. Supporting file formats is not the same as understanding their dependency semantics. [Multi-package model](https://knope.tech/tutorials/releasing-multiple-packages/), [format limitations](https://knope.tech/reference/config-file/packages/) |
| Nx Release | Uses project identity, release groups and ecosystem-specific `VersionActions`/publishers. Its Rust recipe still carries a legacy-versioning restriction, so that documentation alone does not establish current plugin compatibility. | Separate project identity from package metadata, but don’t reproduce Nx’s general build/plugin platform. [Configuration](https://nx.dev/docs/reference/nx-json), [Rust caveat](https://nx.dev/docs/kb/publish-rust-crates) |
| release-please | Supports multiple release strategies and ecosystem-specific workspace plugins. Registry publishing is a separate workflow responsibility. | Keep release ownership, native dependency updates and publication separate. Its documented npm workflow publishes after tags/releases already exist. [Manifest and publishing model](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please/blob/main/docs/manifest-releaser.md) |

My conclusion: Callisto’s useful differentiation is **native-aware, verifiable polyglot release coordination**, not simply supporting more manifest formats.

## What I would correct in our scope

### 1. One authoritative version does not mean one universal version grammar

Maturin can derive the Python distribution’s version from Cargo and convert SemVer to PEP 440. A normal configuration uses `dynamic = ["version"]`; Callisto should not manufacture a second static version field. [Maturin metadata rules](https://www.maturin.rs/metadata)

I tested co-located `Cargo.toml` and `pyproject.toml` with:

- Matching static `1.0.0` versions.
- A Cargo version and a dynamic Python version.

**Both `init` and `status` fail with E007.** The current model rejects mixed canonical-manifest grammars outright. [Current check](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-model/src/package.rs:44)

That means our earlier Rust/Python coverage was incomplete: separate-directory fixtures do not establish support for this common layout.

Recommendation: support the concrete Cargo-owned Maturin case, preserving native version representations and checking built metadata. Do not attempt arbitrary bidirectional conversion between every SemVer and PEP 440 version.

### 2. PyPI completion is an artifact-set question

PyPI creates a release when its **first file** uploads. Further wheels and the sdist are additional uploads under that version. [Upload API](https://docs.pypi.org/api/upload/)

Callisto builds a wheel and sdist, but currently accepts any matching non-yanked file as evidence that the publication is complete. The release preflight then treats that evidence as already satisfied. [Observation](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/registry.rs:499), [preflight](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/mod.rs:325)

Consequently, a partial upload can be skipped on retry. This is source-confirmed; I have not run a live partial-upload experiment.

**This is more important than optional checksum hardening.** We need to know which files this release intended to publish, then confirm that set—not every conceivable wheel platform. PyPI’s index exposes individual filenames, hashes and yank status. [Simple API](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/simple-repository-api/)

### 3. Native dependency syntax must survive normalization

Callisto currently collapses recognized `workspace:` specifications into one generic workspace reference. [Parser](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-manifests/src/npm.rs:517)

But pnpm distinguishes:

- `workspace:*` from an explicit constraint such as `workspace:^1.5.0`.
- A dependency’s alias from its actual package name.
- Relative workspace paths.
- Catalog references whose authoritative value lives elsewhere.

An explicit workspace constraint can fail resolution. pnpm also transforms workspace and catalog references during packing/publication. [Workspace semantics](https://pnpm.io/workspaces), [catalog publishing](https://pnpm.io/catalogs)

Recommendation: retain the resolved distribution, original reference and effective constraint. Let pnpm perform its packing transformations. Where Callisto cannot safely update a reference, disclose that limitation rather than silently treating it as unconstrained.

Canonical IDs still need ecosystem-specific normalization: Python, for example, treats several punctuation/case spellings as the same project. [Python normalization](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/name-normalization/)

### 4. Publication ordering needs explicit ownership

I would retain registry-before-public-announcement as Callisto’s default for today’s ecosystems, but retract any suggestion that it is universally required. Nx’s combined release implementation can create tags and remote releases before publishing. [Nx implementation](https://github.com/nrwl/nx/blob/master/packages/nx/src/command-line/release/release.ts)

A second complication matters now: NAPI’s `prepublishOnly` integration can itself publish platform packages and create/upload GitHub releases. Callisto and those hooks must not independently own the same effects. [NAPI publication behavior](https://napi.rs/docs/cli/pre-publish)

The rule should be:

> Each irreversible effect has one owner. Release completion means all required effects are confirmed—not that a tag exists.

There is no cross-registry transaction to roll back. Recovery should finish missing effects using the original intent and artifacts.

### 5. Future ecosystems need escape room, not implementation now

Two concrete architectural checks are enough to expose major future assumptions:

- **Go:** publishing uses repository tags, and v2+ normally changes the module path. A tag cannot always be placed behind every publication as a completion marker. [Go versioning](https://go.dev/doc/modules/version-numbers)
- **NuGet:** version normalization differs from ordinary SemVer, including removal of build metadata. One package can contain assets selected by runtime identifier and target framework—not just a Rust target triple. [Version rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/concepts/package-versioning), [native assets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/create-packages/native-files-in-net-packages)

Also, registry identity must not imply one endpoint serves every operation. Callisto currently reuses the configured Python endpoint for observation and upload; those are distinct APIs on public PyPI. Private-registry support needs an explicit boundary here. [Index API](https://docs.pypi.org/api/index-api/), [upload API](https://docs.pypi.org/api/upload/)

## The smallest architecture I recommend

Keep four concepts:

1. **Release owner:** what versions/releases together.
2. **Distribution:** canonical ecosystem-qualified identity and native package name.
3. **Version authority:** where the version comes from, with each distribution’s native representation.
4. **Release effects:** required publications/assets/tags/announcements and their prerequisites.

Reuse the existing dependency graph and operation DAG. **Do not introduce five public graph types or a general plugin framework.**

Distinguish these meanings without making them elaborate configuration systems:

- A native package dependency affects native constraints.
- An embedded/build input affects the produced artifact; it does not automatically require publishing that input to its registry.
- Shared versioning is an explicit release policy, not an inferred consequence of either relationship.

Canonical distribution IDs should be used consistently in new machine contracts and authored references. Preserve old references through a deliberate migration path; adding another ecosystem must not silently change historical ownership.

Build tools and CI remain responsible for compiling and packaging. Services, arbitrary interoperability discovery, universal dependency resolution and Go/NuGet publishers stay outside this scope.

## Checks still needed before calling it complete

I would validate a bounded set of representative fixtures:

- Cargo workspace inheritance, renamed dependencies and registry visibility delays.
- npm/pnpm aliases, explicit workspace ranges, catalogs and actual packed metadata.
- Python markers/extras, prereleases, wheel/sdist selection and failure after the first upload.
- NAPI platform packages, lifecycle ownership and clean consumer installation.
- Co-located Maturin projects, Cargo-owned versions and built Python metadata.
- Failure/retry at publication, tag, push, GitHub release and asset-upload boundaries.

Use Go v2 and a multi-runtime NuGet package as **design examples**, not implemented adapters or new release gates.

My recommendation is to proceed with the scoped architecture, amended for **version authority, required artifact sets and single-owner effects**. Those address real problems in today’s systems. Everything more general should wait for a concrete supported use case.

I’ll reconcile the current-behavior specs with the verified findings, then capture the proposed changes in the roadmap and a separate plan. I’ll keep planned behavior out of the specs so they remain an accurate contract for the code we ship today.

I’m using the spec-drift and correction skills to check which claims need updating, and the planning skill to organize the follow-up work. +# Scoped polyglot release model
+
+Status: proposed v1 design, not current behavior. Owner scope: Rust/Cargo, npm/pnpm and Python/PyPI now; leave room for Go and .NET/NuGet without implementing their publishers. Current contracts remain in [the specs](../specs/INDEX.md). Work is sequenced in [the roadmap](../projects/ROAD-TO-V1.md) and [the plan](../projects/V1-SYSTEM-HARDENING.json).
+
+## Four concepts
+
+| Concept | Responsibility | Not equivalent to |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Release owner | Source/version authority and the outputs released together | A display name or registry destination |
+| Distribution | Canonical ecosystem-qualified identity and native package name | A source directory or import/module name |
+| Version authority | Literal or supported inherited/derived source, plus each distribution's native representation | A grammar guessed from a JSON string |
+| Release effect | One required external effect, its destination, evidence and prerequisites | A package tag proving all publications finished |
+
+Keep existing types where they already express these responsibilities. A `PackageKey` locates a directory; it does not prove identity survives a directory move. Do not add opaque IDs or a public plugin protocol without a demonstrated need. The release-owner representation and wire migration must be specified before implementation.
+
+## Canonical references and migration
+
+- New exact references, generated config, changesets and machine reports use `cargo/name`, `npm/@scope/name` or `pypi/name`. Native normalization belongs to the ecosystem; Python distribution names are not import names.
+- Short labels may remain in human output, but never become an alternate identity authority. Ecosystem-specific native names stay available for manifest rewrites and publisher arguments.
+- Legacy bare references are a migration input, not a permanent inference rule for new identities. Resolve only with established ownership; ambiguous input fails with an actionable diagnostic. Specify colon-form compatibility and schema-version support explicitly before changing readers.
+- Adding or removing a same-named sibling, adding a canonical manifest or changing the primary manifest must not transfer another owner's history or regress the last release. A genuine rename/move needs a declared migration boundary, not guessing from current path existence.
+- Keep [ADR 11](../adr/0011-directory-keyed-package-identity.md) in force until [the proposed replacement](../adr/0012-canonical-distribution-release-ownership.md) is implemented and accepted. Do not rename existing tags merely to canonicalize selectors.
+
+## Native versions and dependencies
+
+A release owner can have several distribution outputs. Shared versioning is deliberate; co-location or a build dependency alone does not require version coupling. The initial supported derived-version case is Maturin's Cargo-owned Python version. Preserve `dynamic = ["version"]`, use the known SemVer-to-PEP-440 mapping and verify the built metadata. Do not introduce a universal reversible version converter; unsupported mappings and arbitrary SCM-derived backends need an explicit support decision.
+
+Reuse the native dependency graph and derived release-operation DAG. Preserve each edge's manifest, declared key/alias, resolved distribution, constraint and dependency kind. A native Cargo edge must not become a dependency on every distribution produced by the same source package.
+
+- Native registry dependency: update that ecosystem's reference and derive only relevant publication prerequisites. Range coverage, version cascade and publication order are distinct decisions.
+- Embedded/build input: the consuming artifact needs those bytes or sources. It does not necessarily need that input published to Cargo, npm or PyPI. Builders and CI retain build ordering; add explicit cross-project input relationships only for a supported concrete case.
+- Version coupling: retain fixed/linked policies separately from dependency edges; do not infer a major bump of every wrapper from an internal-language change.
+- Runtime services and arbitrary cross-language discovery are outside the release graph's scope.
+
+For pnpm, retain the difference between `workspace:*`, explicit workspace ranges, aliases, relative paths and catalogs. Let pnpm perform pack-time transformations. For Python, preserve extras, markers and native specifiers; document direct-URL and dynamic-backend support rather than treating them as ordinary ranges. Cargo inherited versions/dependencies require their authoritative root paths in both live and historical reads.
+
+## Effects and completion
+
+For current registry ecosystems, the proposed default is required registry publications confirmed before a shared tag and public GitHub announcement. A draft and uploads may be preparatory effects; public publication waits for all required outputs of that release owner. Exact draft timing must be specified with the implementation. This is Callisto's policy, not a universal ecosystem order.
+
+One physical tag, forge release or upload has one owner even when several distributions share it. One irreversible effect must not be issued by both Callisto and a publishing lifecycle hook. In particular, NAPI `prepublishOnly` can publish platform packages and GitHub assets independently; the supported integration must assign that responsibility once.
+
+A retry retains the authorized roster and observes every remaining effect, even when its tag or some registry files already exist. Keep execution state in memory; the immutable intent, original artifact manifest and providers supply recovery evidence. No journal, automatic version bump, destructive rollback or changed replacement bytes under an already-published version.
+
+PyPI completion is the declared file set for the release, not the first matching wheel or sdist. Required platform packages must exist before their npm owner publishes. Missing, conflicting, yanked and unobservable results must not be collapsed into complete success. Use hashes where needed to distinguish intended files from conflicting bytes; do not make an unapproved universal registry-checksum requirement a v1 gate.
+
+Registry identity is separate from read/upload routes and native authentication configuration. Specify public PyPI first; decide authenticated private indexes and HTML-only indexes explicitly. Mutable npm dist-tags are channel labels, not distribution versions; channel verification/promotion policy is an owner decision, not implicit rollback.

+# 12. Canonical distribution references and explicit release ownership
+
+Status: Proposed
+
+This proposal revises ADR 11's selector promotion and default-tag coupling when implemented. ADR 11 remains the current decision; it is not superseded by this documentation change.
+
+## Context
+
+The owner selected Rust/Cargo, npm/pnpm and Python/PyPI as the current scope, with architectural room for Go and .NET/NuGet. The system audit found that display promotion leaks into dependency rewrites, historical ownership and shared tag/forge ordering. Fresh Cargo/Maturin projects also fail because one package requires one grammar. Evidence and implementation work are recorded in [the findings register](../projects/V1-FINDINGS.md).
+
+## Proposed decision
+
+- Use canonical ecosystem-qualified distribution references for new authored and generated data; native normalization belongs to the ecosystem.
+- Separate release ownership, distribution identity, authoritative version source and external effects. Reuse existing types and graphs; do not add a general plugin framework or opaque IDs without need.
+- Read legacy references through a deliberate compatibility/migration boundary. Preserve historical tag ownership without using display promotion as a release-identity change.
+- Keep native names and manifest context for dependency edits, inherited/derived versions and publisher arguments.
+- Shared external effects have one owner and wait for every required publication/output of that owner. For current ecosystems, public announcement follows registry completion; a future Go source tag can itself be publication.
+- Reruns observe every required effect, including unfinished work after tag creation and missing Python files. Keep ADR 2's committed roster and ADR 3's no-journal recovery.
+
+The exact owner representation, legacy colon-form handling, wire schema migration and channel/private-registry policies must be resolved in the relevant implementation change. This ADR does not approve those unspecified details or introduce release gates.
+
+## Options considered
+
+- Keep collision-triggered bare/qualified identity everywhere: retains inference rules at every new consumer and lets unrelated workspace changes alter identity behavior.
+- Canonicalize one package ID but retain one grammar and per-distribution completion: does not represent Maturin version authority or shared tag/forge effects.
+- Introduce a universal graph/plugin/build system: exceeds the supported use cases and duplicates ecosystem tools.
+
+## Consequences
+
+Pre-v1 breaking references are allowed by the owner requirement, but historical releases and committed decisions still need explicit compatibility. Cargo/npm/Python outputs can share an owner without pretending their native versions or registry evidence are interchangeable. Go/NuGet remain design examples, not shipped adapters.
+

+
+- Owner scope and canonical-identity discussion, 2026-09-26; [REQ-DX-V1](../specs/REQ-DX-V1.md).
+- [Scoped model and primary-source prior art](../architecture/polyglot-v1.md).
+- [System findings and verification limits](../projects/V1-FINDINGS.md).

+
+- NAPI publication hooks can own the same platform/GitHub effects as Callisto. Official hook behavior and Callisto's lifecycle-enabled npm argv establish the risk; a combined generated-workflow fixture is still required (T10).

+- Generated workflows build/place only intended supported outputs and configure native authentication without registry secrets in plan/build jobs. This repo retains no GitHub Environment or separate reviewer gate; the reviewed merge remains the authorization.
+- Fresh-repository runs measure init-to-first-publication against the existing under-ten-minute goal, including commit and credential steps. The supported/unsupported boundary is documented; no timing evidence is claimed until measured.
